claim: There is little agreement about what brain changes accompany motor sequence learning.
source: Despite numerous studies, there is little agreement about what brain changes accompany motor sequence learning, partly because of a general publication bias that favors novel results.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a motivation for the study, reflecting the current state of the literature.

claim: Publication bias favoring novel results has contributed to lack of agreement about brain changes in motor sequence learning.
source: Despite numerous studies, there is little agreement about what brain changes accompany motor sequence learning, partly because of a general publication bias that favors novel results.
evidence: This is stated as a contributing factor to the inconsistency in the literature.

claim: The study included four scanning sessions over 5 weeks of training.
source: We therefore decided to systematically reinvestigate proposed functional magnetic resonance imaging correlates of motor learning in a preregistered longitudinal study with four scanning sessions over 5 weeks of training.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design in the abstract.

claim: Activation decreased more for trained than untrained sequences in premotor and parietal areas.
source: Activation decreased more for trained than untrained sequences in premotor and parietal areas, without any evidence of learning-related activation increases.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in the results section.

claim: There was no evidence of learning-related activation increases.
source: Activation decreased more for trained than untrained sequences in premotor and parietal areas, without any evidence of learning-related activation increases.
evidence: This is a negative finding stated in the abstract and supported by results.

claim: Premotor and parietal regions exhibited changes in fine-grained, sequence-specific activation patterns early in learning.
source: Premotor and parietal regions also exhibited changes in the fine-grained, sequence-specific activation patterns early in learning, which stabilized later.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by pattern component modeling analyses.

claim: Sequence-specific activation patterns in premotor and parietal regions stabilized later in learning.
source: Premotor and parietal regions also exhibited changes in the fine-grained, sequence-specific activation patterns early in learning, which stabilized later.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by correlation analyses across weeks.

claim: No changes were observed in the primary motor cortex (M1).
source: No changes were observed in the primary motor cortex (M1).
evidence: This is a negative finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple analyses in the results.

claim: Human motor sequence learning occurs outside of M1.
source: Overall, our study provides evidence that human motor sequence learning occurs outside of M1.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the pattern of results.

claim: Activity increases cannot be expected as an indicator for learning.
source: Furthermore, it shows that we cannot expect to find activity increases as an indicator for learning, making subtle changes in activity patterns across weeks the most promising fMRI correlate of training-induced plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the absence of activation increases.

claim: Subtle changes in activity patterns across weeks are the most promising fMRI correlate of training-induced plasticity.
source: Furthermore, it shows that we cannot expect to find activity increases as an indicator for learning, making subtle changes in activity patterns across weeks the most promising fMRI correlate of training-induced plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the pattern of results.

claim: Previous studies have reported signal increases in various brain regions with motor sequence learning.
source: Previous studies include reports of signal increases across various brain regions (Floyer-Lea and Matthews, 2005; Grafton et al., 1995; Hazeltine et al., 1997; Karni et al., 1995; Lehéricy et al., 2005; Penhune and Doyon, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies have reported signal decreases with motor sequence learning.
source: as well as signal decreases (Jenkins et al., 1994; Peters et al., 2017; Toni et al., 1998; Ungerleider et al., 2002; Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies have reported nonlinear changes in activation with motor sequence learning.
source: nonlinear changes in activation (Ma et al., 2010; Xiong et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies have reported spatial shifts in activity with motor sequence learning.
source: spatial shifts in activity (Lehéricy et al., 2006; Steele and Penhune, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies have reported changes in multivariate patterns with motor sequence learning.
source: changes in multivariate patterns (Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013; Wymbs and Grafton, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies have reported changes in inter-regional functional connectivity with motor sequence learning.
source: and changes in inter-regional functional connectivity (Bassett et al., 2015; Bassett et al., 2011; Doyon et al., 2002; Mattar et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some motor learning experiments have matched the speed of performance.
source: Additionally, some experiments have matched the speed of performance (Karni et al., 1995; Penhune and Doyon, 2002; Steele and Penhune, 2010; Lehéricy et al., 2005; Seidler et al., 2002; Seidler et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some motor learning experiments have not matched the speed of performance.
source: while others have not (Bassett et al., 2015; Lutz et al., 2004; Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013; Wymbs and Grafton, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: fMRI analysis has many degrees of freedom.
source: Given that fMRI analysis has many degrees of freedom, these inconsistencies may not be too surprising.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of fMRI analysis.

claim: Implicit pressure in the publication system to report findings may have contributed to lack of coherency in motor learning literature.
source: However, the implicit pressure in the publication system to report findings may also have contributed to a lack of coherency.
evidence: This is stated as a potential contributing factor to inconsistencies.

claim: The study design and hypotheses were pre-registered on the Open Science Framework.
source: In order to increase transparency, we pre-registered the design, as well as all tested hypotheses on the Open Science Framework (Berlot et al., 2017; https://osf.io/etnqc)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methodology.

claim: The full dataset is made available to the research community.
source: and make the full dataset available to the research community (Berlot, 2020; OpenNeuro accession number ds002776)
evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.

claim: The primary motor cortex (M1) is the most commonly examined brain region in motor sequence learning.
source: In the context of motor sequence learning, the most commonly examined brain region is the primary motor cortex (M1).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the literature.

claim: Previous reports of increased M1 activation after long-term learning have been interpreted as additional recruitment of neuronal resources for trained behavior.
source: Previous reports of increased M1 activation after long-term learning have been interpreted as additional recruitment of neuronal resources for trained behavior, taken to suggest the skill is represented in M1 (Floyer-Lea and Matthews, 2005; Karni et al., 1995; Karni et al., 1998; Lehéricy et al., 2005; Penhune and Doyon, 2002; for a review see Dayan and Cohen, 2011; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and interpretation.

claim: Several pieces of evidence have suggested that sequence-specific memory may not reside in M1.
source: Since then, several pieces of evidence have suggested that sequence-specific memory may not reside in M1 (Beukema et al., 2019; Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013; Yokoi and Diedrichsen, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some reports studying skill acquisition over a few days may not capture changes that occur over weeks of practice.
source: However, some of these reports studied skill acquisition over a course of a few days, while human skill typically evolves over weeks (and months) of practice.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous studies.

claim: Including several weeks of practice might be more suitable to test whether M1 develops skill-specific representations.
source: Therefore, including several weeks of practice might be more suitable to test whether, and at what time point, M1 develops skill-specific representations.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the study design.

claim: Learning-related activation changes have been reported in premotor and parietal areas.
source: Outside of M1, learning-related activation changes have been reported in premotor and parietal areas (Grafton et al., 2002; Hardwick et al., 2013; Honda et al., 1998; Penhune and Doyon, 2002; Tamás Kincses et al., 2008; Vahdat et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation increases in premotor and parietal areas have been commonly interpreted as increased involvement of these areas in skilled behavior.
source: with activation increases commonly interpreted as increased involvement of these areas in the skilled behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a common interpretation in the literature.

claim: Recent studies have mostly found that activation in premotor and parietal areas predominantly decreases as motor skill develops.
source: Yet, recent studies have mostly found that, as the motor skill develops, activation in these areas predominantly decreases (Penhune and Steele, 2012; Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013; Wu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation reductions could reflect reduced areal involvement in skilled performance.
source: Such reductions are harder to interpret as they could reflect a reduced areal involvement in skilled performance or, alternatively, more energy efficient implementation of the same function (Figure 1b; Picard et al., 2013; Poldrack et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as one possible interpretation, supported by citations.

claim: Activation reductions could reflect more energy efficient implementation of the same function.
source: Such reductions are harder to interpret as they could reflect a reduced areal involvement in skilled performance or, alternatively, more energy efficient implementation of the same function (Figure 1b; Picard et al., 2013; Poldrack et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as an alternative interpretation, supported by citations.

claim: Regional activity increases and decreases could occur simultaneously in the same area.
source: To complicate things further, regional activity increases and decreases could occur simultaneously in the same area (Figure 1c; Steele and Penhune, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility supported by a citation.

claim: Each specific sequence could become associated with a dedicated neuronal subpopulation.
source: A variant of this idea is that each specific sequence becomes associated with dedicated neuronal subpopulation (and hence fMRI activity pattern).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis about sequence representation.

claim: Sequence-specific activation patterns would form the neural correlate of sequence-specific learning.
source: Such a representation would form the neural correlate of sequence-specific learning – the part of the skill that does not generalize to novel, untrained motor sequences (Karni et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical framework, supported by a citation.

claim: Sequence-specific activation patterns should change early in learning when behavior improves most rapidly.
source: Sequence-specific activation patterns should change early in learning (Figure 1d), when behavior improves most rapidly, and stabilize later, once the skill has consolidated and an optimal pattern is established (Peters et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction, supported by a citation.

claim: Sequence-specific patterns should stabilize later in learning once the skill has consolidated.
source: Sequence-specific activation patterns should change early in learning (Figure 1d), when behavior improves most rapidly, and stabilize later, once the skill has consolidated and an optimal pattern is established (Peters et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction, supported by a citation.

claim: Sequence-specific patterns could reorganize by becoming more distinct from one another.
source: One possible way in which sequence-specific patterns could reorganize is by becoming more distinct from one another (Figure 1e; Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis, supported by a citation.

claim: Having a distinctive code for each sequence might allow the system to produce different dynamical sequences while avoiding confusion or 'tangling' of neural trajectories.
source: Having a distinctive code for each sequence might be of particular importance to the system in a trained state, allowing it to produce different dynamical sequences, while avoiding confusion or 'tangling' of the different neural trajectories (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical rationale, supported by a citation.

claim: The study was carried out over 5 weeks of training with 4 sessions of high-field (7 Tesla) fMRI scans.
source: To systematically examine the cortical changes associated with motor sequence learning, we carried out a longitudinal study over 5 weeks of training with 4 sessions of high-field (7 Tesla) fMRI scans.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study design.

claim: Behavioural performance in the first three scanning sessions was imposed to the same speed of performance.
source: Behavioural performance in the first three scanning sessions was imposed to the same speed of performance.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental manipulation.

claim: Matching speed across sessions allows inspection of whether fMRI metrics reflect brain reorganization independent of behavioral change.
source: This allowed us to inspect whether examined fMRI metrics reflect brain reorganization, independent of behavioral change.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the speed-matching design.

claim: Controlling for speed incurs the danger of not tapping into neural resources necessary for skilled performance.
source: However, controlling for speed incurs the danger of not tapping into neural resources that are necessary for skilled performance (Orban et al., 2010; Poldrack, 2000).
evidence: This is stated as a potential limitation, supported by citations.

claim: The study compared fMRI sessions with paced performance at the end of training with one acquired with full speed performance.
source: We therefore compared the fMRI session with paced performance at the end of behavioural training with one acquired with full speed performance (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design.

claim: The manipulation of speed allowed systematic assessment of the role of speed on fMRI metrics of learning.
source: This manipulation allowed us to systematically assess the role of speed on the fMRI metrics of learning, thereby addressing an important methodological problem faced by virtually every study on motor learning.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the design feature.

claim: 26 participants were trained to perform six 9-digit sequences.
source: We trained 26 participants to perform six 9-digit sequences with their right hand on a keyboard device (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study sample and task.

claim: Participants practiced approximately 4000 trials over the course of 5 weeks.
source: Over the course of 5 weeks, participants practiced ~4000 trials (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the training amount.

claim: The average movement time to complete a sequence decreased from an initial 3.2 s to 1.2 s at the end of training.
source: This led to substantial performance improvement, with the average movement time (MT) to complete a sequence decreasing from an initial 3.2 s to 1.2 s at the end of the training (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of behavioral results.

claim: Prior to training, the speed of sequence execution did not differ between trained and untrained sequences.
source: Prior to training (test day 1), the speed of sequence execution did not differ between trained and untrained sequences.
evidence: This is a direct statement of baseline behavioral results.

claim: For all subsequent sessions after training began, movement times were significantly faster for trained than untrained sequences (p<0.001).
source: For all subsequent sessions, MTs were significantly faster for trained than untrained sequences (p<0.001), implying sequence-specific learning.
evidence: This is a direct statement of behavioral results with statistical support.

claim: Performance of trained sequences improved between all subsequent sessions, even after week 3.
source: Additionally, performance of trained sequences improved between all subsequent sessions, even after week 3 (week 3–5: t(25)=5.49, p=1.1e−5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of behavioral results with statistical support.

claim: Participants' performance of trained sequences improved across the five weeks.
source: Thus, participants' performance of trained sequences improved across the five weeks.
evidence: This is a summary statement of behavioral results.

claim: There was no significant change in M1 activation across weeks (F(2,50)=0.44, p=0.85).
source: A region of interest (ROI) analysis of the hand area of M1, contralateral to the performing hand, however, showed no significant change across weeks (F(2,50)=0.44, p=0.85).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from ROI analysis.

claim: There was a significant main effect of sequence type in M1 (F(1,25)=6.32, p=0.019).
source: There was a significant main effect of sequence type (F(1,25)=6.32, p=0.019), but none of the post-hoc t-tests revealed a significant difference.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: The interaction between week and sequence type was not significant in M1 (F(2,50)=0.17, p=0.84).
source: Additionally, the interaction between the two factors was also not significant (F(2,50)=0.17, p=0.84).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: The cosine angle dissimilarity between average trained and untrained patterns in M1 remained unchanged across weeks (F(2,50)=1.71, p=0.19).
source: However, in M1, the averaged cosine angle (Figure 3c) remained unchanged across the weeks (F(2,50)=1.71, p=0.19), indicating that the average activity pattern remained comparable across trained and untrained sequences.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from pattern analysis.

claim: There was no evidence for activation increases, decreases, or relative shifts in activation patterns in M1.
source: In sum, we found no evidence for activation increases (Karni et al., 1995), decreases, or relative shifts in activation patterns (Steele and Penhune, 2010) in M1.
evidence: This is a summary statement of negative findings with citations to contrasting previous reports.

claim: Widespread learning-related reductions in activity were observed in premotor and parietal areas.
source: Instead, we observed widespread learning-related reductions in activity in premotor and parietal areas (Figure 4a), in line with our pre-registered prediction.
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by Figure 4a.

claim: Activation reductions were observed across both subsequent sessions (weeks 1–2, weeks 2–5) for trained and untrained sequences.
source: These activation reductions were observed across both subsequent sessions (i.e. weeks 1–2, weeks 2–5) for trained and untrained sequences, with bigger reductions for trained sequences.
evidence: This is a direct statement of results.

claim: In weeks 2 and 5, trained sequences elicited overall lower activity than untrained sequences.
source: In weeks 2 and 5, trained sequences elicited overall lower activity than untrained sequences (Figure 4b; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for statistical maps).
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by figures.

claim: In PMd, both main effects and interaction were highly significant in a 3 (week) x 2 (sequence type) ANOVA (week: F(2,50)=17.47, p=1.77e−6; sequence type: F(1,25)=11.86, p=2.03e−3; interaction: F(2,50)=13.22, p=2.46e−5).
source: In a 3 (week) x 2 (sequence type) ANOVA on observed activation both main effects and interaction were highly significant in PMd (week: F(2,50)=17.47, p=1.77e−6; sequence type: F(1,25)=11.86, p=2.03e−3; interaction: F(2,50)=13.22, p=2.46e−5)
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: In SPLa, both main effects and interaction were highly significant in a 3 (week) x 2 (sequence type) ANOVA (week: F(2,50)=19.14, p=6.73e-7; sequence type: F(1,25)=19.36, p=1.77e−4; interaction: F(2,50)=21.59, p=1.74e−7).
source: as well as in SPLa (week: F(2,50)=19.14, p=6.73e-7; sequence type: F(1,25)=19.36, p=1.77e−4; interaction: F(2,50)=21.59, p=1.74e−7).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: No main effect of week was observed in S1 (F(2,50)=1.82, p=0.17).
source: In contrast, no main effect of week was observed in S1 (F(2,50)=1.82, p=0.17).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: There was no significant effect of sequence type in S1 (F(1,25)=0.19, p=0.66).
source: Neither was there a significant effect of sequence type (F(1,25)=0.19, p=0.66)
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: There was no significant interaction between week and sequence type in S1 (F(2,50)=2.01, p=0.14).
source: or interaction between the two factors (F(2,50)=2.01, p=0.14).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: Cosine angular dissimilarity between average trained and untrained sequence activation increased significantly across weeks in PMd (F(2,50)=23.63, p=5.98e−8).
source: Both in parietal and premotor areas there was clear evidence for a shift – cosine angular dissimilarity between the average trained and untrained sequence activation increased significantly across weeks (PMd: F(2,50)=23.63, p=5.98e−8
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: Cosine angular dissimilarity between average trained and untrained sequence activation increased significantly across weeks in SPLa (F(2,50)=23.19, p=7.49e−8).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: S1 showed a significant increase in cosine dissimilarity between trained and untrained patterns with learning (F(2,50)=8.68, p=5.79e−4).
source: S1 also showed a significant increase in cosine dissimilarity between trained and untrained patterns with learning (F(2,50)=8.68, p=5.79e−4).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: Changes in cosine dissimilarity in S1 were much less pronounced than those observed in premotor and parietal areas.
source: These changes, however, were much less pronounced than those observed in premotor and parietal areas.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the magnitude of effects.

claim: Before training (week 1), sequences elicit relatively more activation in rostral parts of the premotor and supplementary motor areas.
source: Comparing the pattern of activation revealed that before training (week 1, blue) sequences elicit relatively more activation in rostral parts of the premotor and supplementary motor areas, and that activity was more caudal after training (week 5, red; Figure 5c displays the cross-section of relative activation changes).
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by Figure 5.

claim: Activity was more caudal in premotor areas after training (week 5).
source: Comparing the pattern of activation revealed that before training (week 1, blue) sequences elicit relatively more activation in rostral parts of the premotor and supplementary motor areas, and that activity was more caudal after training (week 5, red; Figure 5c displays the cross-section of relative activation changes).
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by Figure 5.

claim: Activation shifted from more posterior to anterior subregions in posterior parietal cortex after learning.
source: Some differences were also observed in the posterior parietal cortex, with activation shifting from more posterior to anterior subregions after learning (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by Figure 5.

claim: With learning, the execution of sequences relies on slightly different subareas within premotor and parietal regions.
source: Altogether, these results show that with learning, the execution of sequences relies on slightly different subareas within premotor and parietal regions.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the spatial shift results.

claim: Sequence-specific activity patterns were detected in various cortical regions, even in session 1.
source: Consistent with previous results (Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013; Yokoi and Diedrichsen, 2019), we detected sequence-specific activity patterns, i.e. activity patterns that differentiate between the tested motor sequences, in various cortical regions, even in session 1 (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by Figure 6a and citations.

claim: In SPLa, the most likely correlation of activity patterns for trained sequences between weeks 1 and 2 was r = 0.37.
source: In SPLa, the most likely correlation of the activity patterns for the trained sequences between weeks 1 and 2 was r = 0.37.
evidence: This is a direct statement of pattern component modeling results.

claim: In SPLa, for weeks 2–5, the likelihood of correlation for trained sequences peaked at r = 0.6.
source: For week 2–5, the likelihood peaked at r = 0.6.
evidence: This is a direct statement of pattern component modeling results.

claim: For untrained sequences in SPLa, the most likely correlation model was between r = 0.6–0.7 for both week 1–2 and 2–5.
source: In contrast, the likelihood functions for untrained sequences indicated that the most likely model was between r = 0.6–0.7 for both week 1–2 and 2–5.
evidence: This is a direct statement of pattern component modeling results.

claim: The difference in model evidence for trained sequences was significant for correlation between weeks 1–2 in SPLa (t(25)=2.88, p=4.0e−3).
source: The difference in model evidence was significant for correlation between weeks 1–2 in SPLa (t(25)=2.88, p=4.0e−3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: No difference in correlation was observed in SPLa later in learning, between weeks 2 and 5 (t(25)=1.21, p=0.24).
source: In contrast, no difference in correlation was observed later in learning, between weeks 2 and 5 (t(25)=1.21, p=0.24).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: In PMd, correlation of trained sequences was significantly lower than that of untrained sequences between weeks 1 and 2 (t(25)=2.93, p=3.6e−3).
source: A similar pattern of results was observed in PMd, with correlation of trained sequences significantly lower than that of untrained sequences between weeks 1 and 2 (t(25)=2.93, p=3.6e−3)
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: In PMd, no difference in correlation was observed between weeks 2 and 5 (t(25)=0.88, p=0.39).
source: but not between weeks 2 and 5 (t(25)=0.88, p=0.39).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: No change in correlation across weeks 1–2 was observed in M1 (t(25)=0.43, p=0.34).
source: No such change in correlation across weeks 1–2 was observed in M1 (t(25)=0.43, p=0.34).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: In S1, the effect on correlation was just significant (t(25)=1.72, p=0.049).
source: In S1, the effect was just significant (t(25)=1.72, p=0.049).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: Sequence-specific trained patterns in SPLa and PMd reorganize more in weeks 1–2 compared to untrained sequences, and stabilize later with learning.
source: Overall, we found significant evidence that sequence-specific trained patterns in SPLa and PMd reorganize more in weeks 1–2 as compared to the untrained sequences, and stabilize later on with learning, in line with our new pre-registered prediction.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the pattern reorganization results.

claim: No significant change in dissimilarity across weeks was observed in any of the predefined regions.
source: In contrast to our prediction, no significant change in dissimilarity across weeks was observed in any of the predefined regions (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a direct statement of negative results supported by Figure 6d.

claim: The reorganization observed for trained sequences early in learning did not increase the average distinctiveness of the sequence-specific patterns.
source: This suggests that the reorganization observed for trained sequences early in learning did not increase the average distinctiveness of the sequence-specific patterns.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative finding on dissimilarity.

claim: Performance during the 4th scan was 1010 ms faster than in the first session (t(25)=15.7, p=1.82e−14).
source: Performance during the 4th scan was 1010 ms faster than in the first session (t(25)=15.7, p=1.82e−14)
evidence: This is a direct statement of behavioral results with statistical support.

claim: Performance during the 4th scan was 338 ms faster for trained than for untrained sequences (t(25)=9.92, p=4.58e−10).
source: and also 338 ms (t(25)=9.92, p=4.58e−10) faster for trained than for untrained sequences.
evidence: This is a direct statement of behavioral results with statistical support.

claim: Faster performance in the full-speed session led to an increase in activity across premotor and parietal areas.
source: Averaged over trained and untrained sequences, we found that the faster performance in this session led to an increase in activity across premotor and parietal areas (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by Figure 7.

claim: Activation was still lower for trained compared to untrained sequences during full-speed performance, similar to paced performance.
source: Although trained sequences were executed faster than untrained sequences, activation was still lower for trained compared to untrained sequences, similar to what we observed for paced performance (Figure 7c; see Figure 7—figure supplement 1a for statistical maps).
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by figures.

claim: In M1 and S1, there was no difference in activation between trained and untrained sequences during full-speed performance (M1: t(25)=1.78, p=0.09; S1: t(25)=1.69, p=0.10).
source: In M1 and S1, we found no difference in activation between trained and untrained sequences (Figure 7a; M1: t(25)=1.78, p=0.09; S1: t(25)=1.69, p=0.10).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: The pattern of results for evoked activation did not change qualitatively when participants performed at full speed.
source: Overall, the pattern of results for evoked activation did not change qualitatively when participants performed at full speed.
evidence: This is a summary statement comparing paced and full-speed results.

claim: The correlation between sequence-specific patterns across paced and full-speed sessions was relatively high (r = 0.62) across regions of interest.
source: The correlation between sequence-specific patterns was relatively high (r = 0.62) across our regions of interest.
evidence: This is a direct statement of pattern correlation results.

claim: There were no differences in pattern correlation between different cortical regions (F(3,75)=1.47, p=0.23).
source: We found no differences between the different regions (F(3,75)=1.47, p=0.23)
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: There were no differences in pattern correlation between sequence types (trained vs. untrained: F(1,25)=0.25, p=0.62).
source: or sequence types (trained vs. untrained: F(1,25)=0.25, p=0.62).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: The sequence-specific representations activated during full-speed performance are at least partly activated even when performance is slowed down.
source: Thus, the sequence-specific representations activated during performance at high skill level (full speed) are at least partly activated even when performance slowed down.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation results.

claim: Crossnobis dissimilarities increased at full speed for trained sequences in PMd and SPLa.
source: Overall, crossnobis dissimilarities increased at full speed for trained sequences in PMd and SPLa (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by Figure 7e.

claim: No changes in dissimilarity were found in M1 or S1 at full speed.
source: No such changes were found in M1 or S1.
evidence: This is a direct statement of negative results.

claim: Trained sequences showed larger dissimilarities than untrained at full-speed performance across premotor and parietal cortices.
source: Moreover, trained sequences showed larger dissimilarities than untrained at full-speed performance across premotor and parietal cortices (Figure 7f), which was not the case for the last paced session.
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by Figure 7f.

claim: The difference in dissimilarity between trained and untrained sequences was significant for PMd at full speed.
source: In our predefined ROIs, this difference was significant for PMd (Figure 7d)
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results supported by Figure 7d.

claim: Parietal areas showed significantly higher dissimilarities between trained sequences at full speed.
source: but also parietal areas showed significantly higher dissimilarities between trained sequences at full speed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by a supplementary figure.

claim: Dissimilarities based on speed of performance did not differ significantly across trained and untrained sequences (t(25)=0.57, p=0.57).
source: The dissimilarities based on speed of performance did not differ significantly across trained and untrained sequences (t(25)=0.57, p=0.57).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from a control analysis.

claim: Increased dissimilarity of trained compared to untrained patterns in premotor and parietal areas could not be explained by a difference in execution speed.
source: Therefore, increased dissimilarity of trained compared to untrained patterns in premotor and parietal areas could not be explained by a difference in execution speed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the control analysis results.

claim: The increased dissimilarity effect likely reflects changes in activity patterns underlying full speed skilled performance.
source: Instead, this effect likely reflects changes in activity patterns underlying full speed skilled performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dissimilarity results.

claim: No difference in activity between trained and untrained sequences was observed in either putamen or caudate nucleus.
source: Inspecting changes in overall activity across sessions, we observed no difference in activity between trained and untrained sequences in either putamen or caudate nucleus (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by Figure 8a.

claim: The data fail to replicate the result that activation moves from caudate nucleus to putamen with learning.
source: Previous experiments have reported that with learning, activation moves from more 'cognitive' areas of the striatum (i.e. caudate nucleus) to more 'motor' areas (i.e. putamen) (Coynel et al., 2010; Lehéricy et al., 2005; Reithler et al., 2010). Our data fail to replicate this result
evidence: This is a direct statement of negative results with citations to previous reports.

claim: During paced sessions, activity patterns for different sequences were not distinguishable in either caudate nucleus or putamen.
source: During the paced sessions, activity patterns for different sequences were not distinguishable in either caudate nucleus or putamen (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of results supported by Figure 8c.

claim: During full speed performance, trained sequences elicited distinct activity patterns in both caudate nucleus and putamen (caudate nucleus: t(25)=2.27, p=0.032; putamen: t(25)=2.44, p=0.022).
source: However, during full speed performance trained sequences elicited distinct activity patterns in both regions (i.e. crossnobis dissimilarity >0: caudate nucleus: t(25)=2.27, p=0.032; putamen: t(25)=2.44, p=0.022; Figure 8c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results supported by Figure 8c.

claim: The effect of distinct patterns in striatum was specific to trained sequences, with untrained sequences still exhibiting undistinguishable patterns at full speed.
source: This effect was specific to the trained sequences, with untrained sequences still exhibiting undistinguishable patterns of activity at full speed.
evidence: This is a direct statement of results.

claim: Trained motor sequences are represented in the form of distinct activity patterns in the striatum during full speed skilled performance.
source: Thus, we found some evidence that trained motor sequences are represented in the form of distinct activity patterns in the striatum during full speed skilled performance.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the striatal results.

claim: The correlation between sequence-specific patterns in putamen across paced and full speed sessions was higher than 0 (t(25)=9.56, p=8.0e−10).
source: The correlation between sequence-specific patterns in both regions was higher than 0 (putamen: t(25)=9.56, p=8.0e−10
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: The correlation between sequence-specific patterns in caudate across paced and full speed sessions was higher than 0 (t(25)=6.37, p=1.1e−6).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: The correlation between sequence-specific patterns in putamen across paced and full speed sessions was lower than 1 (t(25)=8.85, p=3.6e−9).
source: but lower than 1 (putamen: t(25)=8.85, p=3.6e−9
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: The correlation between sequence-specific patterns in caudate across paced and full speed sessions was lower than 1 (t(25)=5.86, p=4.1e−6).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results.

claim: Moving faster engages similar representations as moving slower in the striatum, but helps to increase the signal-to-noise ratio.
source: This suggests that moving faster engages similar representations as moving slower, but helps to increase the signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation results.

claim: The lack of observable change in M1 activation contradicts some prior results showing increased M1 activation for matched performance after learning.
source: On the one hand, our lack of any observable change in M1 activation contradicts some prior results, where increased activation in M1 was observed for matched performance after learning (Karni et al., 1995; Matsuzaka et al., 2007; Penhune and Doyon, 2002; Steele and Penhune, 2010; Vahdat et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a comparison of current results with previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: The lack of M1 changes does not align with reports of M1 stimulations influencing consolidation or storage of motor skills.
source: and does not align with reports of M1 stimulations influencing consolidation or storage of motor skills (in motor sequence tasks: Kang and Paik, 2011; Nitsche et al., 2003; Reis et al., 2009; Waters-Metenier et al., 2014; in other motor tasks: Classen et al., 1998; Galea et al., 2011; Hadipour-Niktarash et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison of current results with previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: The results suggest that the pattern of neural activity in M1 does not change as participants become more skilled at producing motor sequences.
source: Instead, our results suggest that the pattern of neural activity in M1 does not change as participants become more skilled at producing motor sequences.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the M1 results.

claim: The M1 results are consistent with recent evidence demonstrating that M1 does not change activation with learning.
source: This is consistent with a recent line of evidence demonstrating that M1 does not change activation with learning (Huang et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature, supported by a citation.

claim: M1 primarily encodes single movement elements, rather than sequences.
source: and primarily encodes single movement elements, rather than sequences (Yokoi et al., 2018; Russo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of M1 function, supported by citations.

claim: Activity increases related to faster movement speeds are compensated for by the shorter duration spent on the task in M1.
source: This suggests that the activity increases related to faster movement speeds are compensated for by the shorter duration spent on the task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the full-speed results in M1.

claim: S1 is involved during consolidation of motor skills.
source: This is consistent with a recent study demonstrating that S1, but not M1, is involved during consolidation of motor skills (Kumar et al., 2019; for a review on somatosensory plasticity in motor learning see Ostry and Gribble, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: The result of activation decreases contrasts with previous studies reporting increases in activation in premotor areas with learning.
source: This result contrasts with other previous studies reporting increases in activation in premotor areas with learning (Grafton et al., 2002; Honda et al., 1998; Penhune and Doyon, 2002; Vahdat et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Publication bias may be partially responsible for inconsistencies in reports of signal changes with learning.
source: Partially responsible for these inconsistencies may be a publication bias, favoring reports of signal increases over signal decreases with learning.
evidence: This is stated as a potential explanation for literature inconsistencies.

claim: The data corroborate recent studies reporting reduced activation in task-evoked premotor and parietal areas.
source: Our data corroborate a number of recent studies reporting reduced activation in task-evoked premotor and parietal areas (Steele and Penhune, 2010; Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013; Wu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Activation increases for trained relative to untrained sequences were observed in areas suppressed below baseline during sequence execution.
source: The only activation increases for trained relative to untrained sequences were observed in areas that were suppressed below baseline during sequence execution.
evidence: This is a direct statement of results.

claim: Decreased inhibition of the default mode network likely reflects central attentional resources being freed up.
source: Our observation of decreased inhibition of the default mode network likely reflects central attentional resources being freed up, allowing participants to engage in other mental processes (e.g., daydreaming) while performing the task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the default mode network results.

claim: Release from initial deactivation in default mode network is possibly task-irrelevant, reflecting increased automaticity with learning.
source: Thus, this release from initial deactivation is possibly task-irrelevant, reflecting increased automaticity with learning (Shamloo and Helie, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Changes in sequence-specific activity patterns constitute a more likely fMRI correlate of sequence-specific performance advantage than changes in average activation.
source: As a more direct fMRI metric of plasticity, we suggest to inspect changes in the sequence-specific activity patterns, since these constitute a more likely fMRI correlate of the sequence-specific performance advantage observed after training.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological recommendation based on the results.

claim: The finding of early plasticity and later stabilization resonates with animal studies suggesting similar patterns in neuronal activity.
source: This finding resonates with several animal studies suggesting that the emergence of skilled behavior is associated with early plasticity and later stabilization of neuronal activity patterns (Makino et al., 2017; Peters et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: The study advances animal findings by demonstrating that reorganization occurs at the level of sequence-specific patterns.
source: Here we report a similar effect in humans, and advance these findings by demonstrating that this reorganization occurs at the level of sequence-specific patterns.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the current study.

claim: By pacing participants' speed, the study was able to cleanly dissociate changes in organization of activity patterns from changes in behavioral performance or variability.
source: Additionally, by pacing participants' speed, we were able to cleanly dissociate changes in the organization of activity patterns from changes in the behavioral performance or variability.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological advantage of the study design.

claim: Engagement of specific neuronal subpopulations for different sequences is particularly important when pushing the limit of performance.
source: This indicates that the engagement of specific neuronal subpopulations for different sequences is particularly important when pushing the limit of performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the full-speed dissimilarity results.

claim: The striatum has been suggested to play a critical role in skilled performance.
source: While our study focused on the role of cortical areas in motor sequence learning, we also examined activation in the striatum, which has been suggested to play a critical role in skilled performance (Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Kawai et al., 2015; Otchy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as background from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: The finding of differential sequence-specific activity patterns in striatum is in line with a recent report showing distinguishable striatal patterns for consolidated motor sequences.
source: Nonetheless, we observed distinguishable striatal activation patterns for different trained sequences at full speed, in line with a recent report showing distinguishable striatal patterns for performance of consolidated motor sequences (Pinsard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The finding of differential patterns is a necessary condition for a functional role of the striatum in production of skilled behaviors.
source: While by itself the finding of differential sequence-specific activity patterns is not evidence for a causal role of the striatum in the production of skilled behaviors, it is a necessary condition for such a functional role.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference about the implications of the results.

claim: The results are in line with the proposed involvement of the striatum in motor sequence learning.
source: Therefore, our results here are in line with the proposed involvement of the striatum in motor sequence learning.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the striatal results.

claim: Full speed performance might be particularly important for studies of striatal multivariate activation to counteract lower signal-to-noise ratio.
source: Additionally, our results suggest that full speed performance might be particularly important for further studies of striatal multivariate activation to counteract the generally lower signal-to-noise ratio in this region.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological recommendation based on the results.

claim: In terms of overall fMRI activation, the pattern of results remained the same for paced vs. full speed performance.
source: Our results provide two important insights: first, in terms of the overall fMRI activation, the pattern of results remained the same for paced vs. full speed performance.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the speed comparison results.

claim: Increased motor demands and decreased time on task averaged out in the full-speed condition.
source: This indicates that, in this specific case, the increased motor demands and the decreased time on task averaged out.
evidence: This is an interpretation of why activation patterns were similar across speeds.

claim: Paced performance may be a better choice when comparing overall activation across sessions.
source: In general, however, these two factors may not balance perfectly – therefore paced performance may be a better choice when comparing overall activation across sessions.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological recommendation.

claim: Sequence-specific activation patterns were much stronger when performing at maximal speeds compared to slow and paced performance.
source: Second, even though slow and paced performance in the trained state activated sequence-specific activation patterns, these were much stronger when performing at maximal speeds.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the pattern strength results.

claim: For questions regarding fine-grained patterns, it might be more suitable to challenge the system fully.
source: Thus, for questions regarding the fine-grained patterns, it might be more suitable to challenge the system fully.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological recommendation based on the results.

claim: The dataset can serve as a resource for other researchers to test novel predictions about learning related changes.
source: However, we hope that our dataset can serve as a resource for other researchers to (re-)test novel predictions about learning related changes.
evidence: This is stated as a goal for data sharing.

claim: Historically, the question of neural substrates of learning was simplified by studying activation increases in single areas as proxies for motor 'engram' localization.
source: Historically, the question was simplified by studying activation increases in single areas as proxies for motor 'engram' localization (Lashley, 1950; Berlot et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as historical context, supported by citations.

claim: Subtler changes in distributed patterns of fMRI activity have the potential to provide more direct metrics of plasticity.
source: In contrast, subtler changes in the distributed patterns of fMRI activity have the potential to provide more direct metrics of plasticity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about methodological approaches.

claim: Increased pattern reorganization and larger pattern separation for trained sequences may be useful as general fMRI correlates of neural reorganization beyond motor learning.
source: Increased pattern reorganization (across weeks), and larger pattern separation for trained sequences was found across prefrontal, parietal, and striatal regions. These metrics may be useful as general fMRI correlates of neural reorganization beyond the domain of motor learning.
evidence: This is stated as a broader implication of the findings.
